subject: operating-systems
title: Race conditions and ordering
summary: A race condition occurs when correctness depends on an uncontrolled relative ordering of concurrent operations.

questions.prompt: When is a data race possible?
options: Conflicting accesses to shared data overlap without required synchronization
Two constants have the same value
A process reads its own local variable
questions.answerKey: Unsynchronized conflicting accesses can interleave unpredictably.
questions.explanation: Read-only sharing is not a data race.

questions.prompt: What makes a check-then-act sequence unsafe?
options: The checked condition can change before the action uses it
questions.answerKey: Another thread can modify the state between the check and the action.
questions.explanation: The pair must be atomic or protected by an appropriate synchronization discipline.

questions.prompt: A thread checks queue-not-empty, is preempted, and another thread removes the final item. What bug can follow?
options: The first thread may remove from an empty queue
questions.answerKey: The predicate was stale when the first thread performed the removal.
questions.explanation: A lock or condition-variable protocol must protect and recheck the predicate.

questions.prompt: Why is printing a shared variable sometimes misleading during a race investigation?
options: The print itself can change timing and hide or expose the race
Output is always atomic with all memory accesses
It proves the program is correct
questions.answerKey: Instrumentation perturbs scheduling and may alter the observed interleaving.
questions.explanation: Repeatable output is not proof of absence of a race.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between mutual exclusion and ordering synchronization.
questions.answerKey: Mutual exclusion prevents conflicting critical sections from overlapping. Ordering synchronization establishes that one event happens before another, such as a consumer waiting until a producer publishes data; a program may need both.
questions.explanation: A lock alone does not necessarily express that a particular event has occurred.

questions.prompt: Give a correct strategy for protecting a shared counter and explain why it works.
questions.answerKey: Guard the read-modify-write increment with a mutex, or use an atomic increment operation with the required memory semantics. The operation then cannot interleave with another conflicting increment, preserving the counter update invariant.
questions.explanation: Simply declaring a variable volatile does not generally make increment atomic.
